 Now that Democrats are set to control the Pennsylvania House, Senate, and the Governor's Residence, Governor Josh Shapiro said their first priority should be to pass an increase in the minimum wage.
 He posted on social media that he supports increasing it from $7.25 to $15 an hour, but newly elected State Sen. Mark Pinsley said they should go bigger.
 "I am going to fight hard right now for $25 an hour," said Pinsley.
 $25 would make Pennsylvania's minimum wage the highest in the nation, and Pinsley argued, they should roll it out quickly.
 "I'm not saying to do that jump overnight; I'm just saying it doesn't need to be very slow. It can happen over a several-year period of time, rather than it being 10 years," said Pinsley.
 But the State Senator Pinsley is replacing, Jarrett Coleman, said an increase like that could be disastrous.
 "I spoke to small businesses in the Lehigh Valley, for example, that even at 15 dollars an hour, they will lay off workers here," said Coleman.
 Coleman said, in addition to cutting jobs, he thinks companies will have to raise prices.
 "Those that do increase the minimum wage are going to offset the cost. They're going to increase the cost of goods and services," said Coleman.
 But Pinsley said he's not convinced that will happen.
 "If you look at New York, New Jersey, Seattle, there has been little to no inflation due to this. I'm not saying none, but little to no inflation," said Pinsley.
 But there is one area where they both agree: ending what's known as "state preemption" and allowing counties to set their own minimum wage. Coleman even wrote a bill on the subject.
 "It was called the Fairness in Wages Act, which would allow counties to set their individual wages that would be representative of those areas," said Coleman.
 "If we were to change preemption, that would allow individual counties to raise the minimum wage within their borders," said Pinsley.
 Pinsley also argues, wherever the minimum wage is finally set, it should be indexed to inflation, allowing it to increase every year by a small percentage on its own so lawmakers never have to have this discussion again.
 "Whatever the minimum wage is, attach a cost-of-living adjustment to it every year," said Pinsley.
